overview: Unangax̂ communities belong to the Aleutian Islands and western Alaska Peninsula. The imported outline shows only an eastern portion of their homeland, leaving out much of the island chain. Aleut is a later name introduced by outsiders. This card includes later history across the wider homeland and the Pribilof communities established under Russian colonial rule; they are not all settlements shown in the 1492 outline.

periods.title: Long island histories
periods.summary: Early stoneworking sites and later villages preserve thousands of years of life beside the sea.

periods.title: Russian colonial rule
periods.summary: Fur trading brought coercion, disease and forced labor, including relocation to the Pribilof Islands.

periods.title: American rule and written language
periods.summary: Communities experienced new administration while Unangam Tunuu literacy and teaching developed.

periods.title: War, return and cultural work
periods.summary: Forced wartime displacement was followed by continuing community life and cultural education.

items.text: At Anangula, near Umnak, a stoneworking site is about 9,000 years old. Craftspeople struck long, narrow blades from stone cores and sharpened some with smaller flakes. Chert, shale, basalt-andesite and obsidian came from beyond the immediate site. Later volcanic ash covered the workshop.

Anangula also has a younger village, separate from the ancient blade-making site. Archaeologists recorded up to twenty-four house depressions in three rows beside a bluff, with smaller storage pits. A stream supplied fresh water. The ground still preserves a neighborhood plan long after its roofs disappeared.

Russian expeditions reached the region in 1741, followed by fur hunters. Violence, disease and forced hunting disrupted communities and reduced their ability to gather food for themselves. Unangax̂ expertise at sea became something colonial traders exploited.

After finding the Pribilof seal rookeries in 1786 and 1787, Russians compelled Aleutian villagers to work there. Seasonal camps became permanent communities by the early nineteenth century. Under later American administration, federal officials controlled employment, travel and even marriages on the islands.

An ulax̂ was partly dug into the earth, with a wooden or whalebone frame and a grass-and-sod roof. Many were entered down a ladder through the roof. From outside, the home could look like a grassy mound. The roof doubled as the route to the front door.

The National Park Service’s historical account describes maternal kinship: children belonged to their mother’s extended family, and women owned homes. Maternal uncles had important roles in teaching boys hunting and cultural practices. Family education involved a wider circle than parents alone.

The iqyax kayak joined a light frame with a waterproof skin covering. Driftwood, bone and sinew could go into the framework, while women’s careful waterproof stitching helped seal the vessel. Hunting at sea depended on skilled sewing as well as skilled paddling.

A parka from Attu Island, collected between 1891 and 1898, is made from seal intestines. In a 2003 museum discussion, elders explained cleaning, inflating and drying the material before cutting it into strips. Sewn with sinew, the strips made a remarkably light waterproof garment.

The raincoat’s details matter: double-folded seams kept water out, a separately sewn hood had a face drawstring, and colored yarn decorated the seams. A kayaker could wear such a parka with a spray skirt sealing the cockpit. Staying dry was an engineering problem solved with patient needlework.

In 1942, American authorities removed 881 Unangax̂ from nine villages to southeast Alaska. Atka families saw American troops burn their homes and church to prevent Japanese use. This forced removal was distinct from the Japanese capture of Attu residents, who became prisoners overseas.

Many evacuees were confined in abandoned industrial camps with contaminated water, inadequate medical care and no proper toilets or bathing facilities. People repaired buildings, installed water and electricity, and found work despite restrictions. Unalaska residents built a makeshift church, preserving a community gathering place amid displacement.

Beginning in 1824, Ivan Veniaminov worked with Unangax̂ speakers on a writing system and religious and educational translations. Later, Knut Bergsland collaborated with speakers including William Dirks Sr. and Moses Dirks on modern writing and teaching resources. A major dictionary appeared in 1994 and a grammar in 1997.

The community food program prints this Eastern Unangam Tunuu sample: “Qaqamiiĝux̂ qalgadam ukulganaa ngiin ugutaasakun”. Its English heading reads, “Subsistence is sustenance for the life.” This modern written sentence connects food gathering with living well; it is a community teaching example rather than an ancient inscription.

A preschool food curriculum developed in 2016 combines Unangam Tunuu listening lessons, harvest pictures, recipes, coloring pages and family letters. Its six units include fish, marine mammals, plants and tidal foods. Children can learn local food words while families contribute recipes and foods from home.

The Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association’s cultural heritage department, formed in 1998, preserves language, art, historical places and cultural objects. Its work joins recording older knowledge with teaching younger generations. A museum collection, a language lesson and care for an archaeological site can support the same community effort.

ending.text: The map’s 1500 endpoint is only a coverage cutoff. Colonial exploitation and wartime displacement transformed Unangax̂ life, but communities, cultural programs and language teaching continue. The history has no single fall or disappearance.
